practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult abruptly becomes unresponsive in an ED waiting area. Which action best reflects the first educational priority in this course?

options.text: Obtain a detailed medication reconciliation before calling for help.
Activate the resuscitation response, assess responsiveness/breathing/pulse per local protocol, and begin team-based resuscitation as indicated.
Wait for a complete history to decide whether the event is cardiac.
Move the patient to a private room before assessing them.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Sudden unresponsiveness is a high-acuity presentation. Current resuscitation guidance supports immediate recognition and team response; diagnosis is refined during resuscitation, not before it. This is an educational question, not a substitute for current local protocol or certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with acute dyspnea has hypotension and altered mentation. Which reasoning error is most unsafe?

options.text: Treating the presentation as high acuity while evaluating respiratory, cardiac, obstructive and distributive causes.
Reassessing oxygenation, ventilation, perfusion and mental status after interventions.
Anchoring on anxiety because the patient appears frightened before assessing physiologic threats.
Escalating early to a resuscitation-capable team.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The course uses a threat-first approach to undifferentiated presentations. Anxiety can coexist with serious illness and cannot safely exclude it. The emergency-care framework emphasizes systematic assessment and reassessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient develops sudden focal weakness and speech difficulty. Which handoff detail is especially time-sensitive to document and communicate?

options.text: The patient’s preferred television program.
Last-known-well time and symptom timeline, plus relevant medication history and baseline function when available.
A definitive stroke subtype before imaging.
A promise that the patient will receive a particular intervention.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Emergency stroke evaluation depends on an accurate time course and critical history. The CDC emphasizes urgent EMS activation and hospital evaluation; this course does not teach treatment eligibility or provide a therapeutic directive.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes point-of-care ultrasound in this independent-study course?

options.text: Watching a video establishes competence to perform invasive ultrasound-guided procedures alone.
It is a useful framework for learning application categories, anatomy, image limits and interpretation; acquisition and procedures require supervised training and local credentialing.
It replaces clinical examination and all other imaging.
Only cardiac views are within emergency medicine scope.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABEM lists resuscitative, diagnostic and procedural applications, while ACEP’s Sonoguide discusses application-specific technique and precautions. Neither source makes viewing material a credential. The course therefore restricts this work to conceptual/image-based study.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional febrile patient has new confusion and poor peripheral perfusion. Which course action is most appropriate?

options.text: Label the patient “simple viral illness” and defer reassessment.
Recognize a possible high-risk infection trajectory, escalate urgently, collect focused clinical information and use the institution’s current evidence-based pathway.
Use a generic online lecture as a complete treatment order.
Wait until a single laboratory value proves the diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC describes sepsis programs as supporting recognition, evidence-based management, recovery and tracking. The course deliberately avoids prescribing medications or doses and directs learners to local protocols and supervision.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient after a fall has neck pain and evolving weakness. What is the best first course framing?

options.text: Delay escalation until a learner independently decides on a final diagnosis.
Use an organized trauma assessment, protect against further harm according to current local protocol, and escalate for supervised trauma evaluation.
Ask the patient to walk repeatedly to test the weakness.
Rely on a single historical feature to exclude injury.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The WHO emergency-care materials organize trauma resuscitation and referral, while ABEM identifies trauma and procedures as core domains. Independent study cannot authorize immobilization, imaging or trauma treatment decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional bystander reports an unknown-pill exposure with declining alertness. Which additional history most directly improves early toxicologic reasoning?

options.text: Route, timing, formulation, estimated amount, co-ingestants and available container information.
Only the patient’s favorite food.
A certainty that every exposure has the same antidote.
A decision to omit poison-center or toxicology consultation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A structured exposure history limits anchoring and helps a supervised team seek expert support. CDC’s outpatient opioid guidance is not a universal toxicology protocol, so the question does not infer a drug-specific treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately reflects ABEM board eligibility boundaries?

options.text: Completion of this course establishes ABEM board eligibility.
Eligibility begins after graduation when a Program Director verifies completed training and ABEM verifies licensure requirements; the course cannot provide either.
Any online video series substitutes for accredited residency training.
Board eligibility has no time limit.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABEM states that a graduate of an ACGME-, RCPSC- or ACEM-accredited EM program or ABEM-approved combined program, with licensure requirements fulfilled, may become board eligible after Program Director verification. ABEM describes a five-year eligibility period ending December 31 of the final year.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional parent is distressed while a child is being evaluated. What communication action is most consistent with the course?

options.text: Avoid questions because family members are always disruptive.
Use clear, empathic, patient-/family-centered communication while maintaining safety, privacy and team coordination.
Promise outcomes before the assessment is complete.
Exclude the caregiver from all history taking.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABEM’s Certifying Exam identifies patient-centered communication, difficult conversations and conflict management as assessed skills. The correct answer does not create a legal rule or replace local policy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner wants to place a source-hosted CT image from an online case into a paid educational product. What is the safest response?

options.text: Copy it because free viewing always permits any reuse.
Check the individual source licence and obtain permission where needed; use a link rather than rehosting if licence/scope is uncertain.
Remove attribution to make reuse easier.
Generate a fake scan and present it as a patient image.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia’s cases have a CC BY-NC-SA licence with attribution and non-commercial conditions, and its licence page specifically excludes paid courses without a separate arrangement. This course links to, rather than copies, source-hosted cases and never creates synthetic diagnostic scans.

title: Interventional Pulmonary Fellowship Training Program
prerequisites: Educational level: advanced learner already grounded in internal medicine, pulmonary physiology, thoracic imaging, basic bronchoscopy concepts, evidence appraisal, and patient safety.

Formal fellowship entry is different from this course: the joint IP requirements page states completion of an ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited pulmonary or pulmonary-critical-care fellowship and says candidates should have completed a 3-year PCCM or 2-year pulmonary program and be ABIM board-certified or eligible in pulmonary medicine. Confirm live requirements with programs.

No learner should attempt bronchoscopy, pleural procedures, sedation/anesthesia management, radiation-guided interventions, or device use from course materials. Those require supervised clinical training, local privilege, equipment-specific training, and institutional policy.
objectives: Map study to the published AABIP IP Board blueprint while distinguishing blueprint, certification policy, fellowship accreditation, and institutional curriculum.
Interpret guideline-based concepts in EBUS specimen acquisition, CAO, pleural disease, screening/nodule evaluation, and BLVR boundaries.

Appraise public recordings for access, sponsorship, currency, and duration evidence.
Use authentic, de-identified, appropriately licensed imaging data only under stated terms and without rehosting unlicensed material.
Document uncertainty, escalation triggers, and educational limits in fictional case analyses.

Peripheral pulmonary nodules, screening, navigation, and image guidance
Central airway obstruction: triage, etiologies, and therapeutic strategy
Rigid bronchoscopy, dilation, foreign bodies, and airway stents
coveredTopics: migration, mucus plugging, granulation, removal planning

unitMap.text: Endobronchial ablation and multidisciplinary cancer care
Pleural imaging, ultrasound, thoracentesis, and tube principles
Pleural infection, pneumothorax, fistulae, and persistent air leak
Malignant pleural effusion, pleuroscopy, IPCs, and palliation
COPD bronchoscopic interventions and transplant airway complications
Professional practice: research appraisal, coding boundaries, quality, and career development

topicGaps: No duration-verified, accessible long-form teaching ledger sufficient to cover rigid bronchoscopy/anesthesia/rescue, stent and dilation strategy, detailed ablation modality tradeoffs, transplant airway complications, or BLVR selection and follow-up; the newly found recordings do not close these domains.

Pleural recordings are now better represented, including a 56:50 ATS panel on current controversies, but dedicated source-grounded teaching remains needed for pleural infection pathways, procedural safety, pleuroscopy, IPC/pleurodesis choices and complication surveillance; pair dated recordings with the valid BTS 2023 documents.

Peripheral nodule, CBCT and radiation-safety recordings are now verified; however, their evidence is limited, some are sponsored, technology-specific or based on small/single-center series. Independent comparative evidence, current screening eligibility and radiation protection remain required.

The public WABIP day-one full event has a directly observed runtime but the page exposes only a broad event title, not a detailed agenda; it is mapped only to broad IP scope and is not treated as evidence for each procedure topic.

AABIP member-library webinars that directly address anesthesia, stents, ablation, pleural infection, BLVR, transplant and coding remain login-restricted and are not counted. Public transcripts without directly observed player totals remain excluded.
Observed video time is not clinical training. Rotations, case volume, conferences, unsupervised skills, assessment of competency and actual clinical practice are not counted as recordings.

medical.boardStatus: AABIP publishes an Initial IP Board Certification examination and a 2025-updated blueprint. AABIP’s 2026 accredited-fellowship application pathway requires successful completion of an accredited IP fellowship, an IP fellowship certificate, program-director attestation, general pulmonary board certification, and a valid state medical license; it says procedure logs are not required for that application and reserves amendment/audit authority. Separately, AABIP’s April 22, 2026 accreditation-status page lists Johns Hopkins University as ACGME Accredited and states that graduates must graduate from an AABIP/AIPPD- or ACGME-accredited program on the day of graduation to be IP board-eligible. ABIM’s July 31, 2026 update says IP subspecialty certification was still in evaluation/potential development; no ABIM IP certificate or exam is claimed here.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study course does not provide ACGME training, a fellowship certificate, program-director attestation, procedural logs, supervised competency assessment, a valid state license, ABIM pulmonary certification, AABIP eligibility, ABMS/ABIM IP certification, credentialing, privileges, or licensure. Requirements change; verify directly with the certifier and training program. Passing this course cannot predict or guarantee passing any examination.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Medicine
officialProgrammes.name: Ko Pen Wang Interventional Pulmonary Fellowship (directory label: Interventional Pulmonary Fellowship Training Program)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The fellowship directory currently labels it ACGME Accredited, 1 year, with two one-year positions and optional additional research year. The program page calls it the Ko Pen Wang fellowship and describes 12 months of advanced clinical IP training in diagnostic bronchoscopy, therapeutic airway and pleural procedures; bi-monthly conference/national meetings, weekly IP clinic and chest tumor board; and an optional 12-month research year. The page does not disclose a fixed rotation calendar, detailed case-volume requirements, named service rotations, or protected didactic-hour total—none are inferred.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This is an actual separate Johns Hopkins clinical physician fellowship, not a generic directory category. Scope is a transparent independent-study companion to interventional pulmonology knowledge. It does not reproduce the Johns Hopkins curriculum, claim affiliation, or convert recordings/readings into clinical training.
sourceCaveats: Institutional program pages, ACGME accreditation, AABIP certification, and ABIM/ABMS certification are different source types; they are not interchangeable.

The ACGME-hosted joint requirements URL includes historical/proposal-era material; it is used for educational-entry context, not to assert live program accreditation. Current Johns Hopkins status is checked at Hopkins and AABIP’s 2026 listing.
AABIP’s historical board-certification overview is dated 2017; current application requirements are taken instead from the updated 2026 application page.
Public lectures are not a complete official curriculum and several potentially relevant AABIP webinar-library items require member login. Those are named as inaccessible, not counted.

YouTube metadata/access can change. Durations are counted only where a direct public player total was observed on the identified video ID; sponsored recordings are flagged and not treated as guideline authority.
No proprietary exam questions, paid resources, exam recalls, patient records, fabricated scans, or unlicensed image rehosting are included.

topicGaps: No duration-verified, accessible long-form teaching ledger sufficient to cover rigid bronchoscopy/anesthesia/rescue, stent and dilation strategy, detailed ablation modality tradeoffs, transplant airway complications, or BLVR selection and follow-up; the newly found recordings do not close these domains.

Pleural recordings are now better represented, including a 56:50 ATS panel on current controversies, but dedicated source-grounded teaching remains needed for pleural infection pathways, procedural safety, pleuroscopy, IPC/pleurodesis choices and complication surveillance; pair dated recordings with the valid BTS 2023 documents.

Peripheral nodule, CBCT and radiation-safety recordings are now verified; however, their evidence is limited, some are sponsored, technology-specific or based on small/single-center series. Independent comparative evidence, current screening eligibility and radiation protection remain required.

The public WABIP day-one full event has a directly observed runtime but the page exposes only a broad event title, not a detailed agenda; it is mapped only to broad IP scope and is not treated as evidence for each procedure topic.

AABIP member-library webinars that directly address anesthesia, stents, ablation, pleural infection, BLVR, transplant and coding remain login-restricted and are not counted. Public transcripts without directly observed player totals remain excluded.
Observed video time is not clinical training. Rotations, case volume, conferences, unsupervised skills, assessment of competency and actual clinical practice are not counted as recordings.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional trainee is reviewing the 2025 AABIP IP Board Exam Blueprint. Which statement best describes the two primary domains?

options.text: Disease-specific knowledge 75%; procedural knowledge 25%.
Disease-specific knowledge 50.4%; procedural knowledge 49.6%.
Procedural knowledge 60%; disease-specific knowledge 40%.
The blueprint does not report domain weights.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published blueprint reports disease-specific knowledge at 50.4% and procedural knowledge at 49.6%. This is a study-planning fact, not an examination item.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional educational vignette, a patient has symptomatic malignant central airway obstruction. Which option most accurately reflects the 2024 CHEST guideline-in-focus page?

options.text: Therapeutic bronchoscopy should replace all systemic therapy and radiation.
Therapeutic bronchoscopy is suggested as an adjunct to systemic medical therapy and/or local radiation; rigid bronchoscopy is suggested over flexible bronchoscopy for therapeutic interventions.
Moderate sedation is required over deep sedation/general anesthesia for every therapeutic bronchoscopy.
CT has no role in CAO evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CHEST states therapeutic bronchoscopy is suggested as an adjunct, suggests rigid over flexible bronchoscopy for therapeutic interventions, and suggests general anesthesia/deep sedation over moderate sedation. Application depends on expertise and patient context.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a fictional patient with suspected malignant disease undergoing EBUS-TBNA, which specimen-acquisition approach is aligned with the 2024 CHEST guideline-in-focus page?

options.text: Use a 19-gauge needle preferentially and stop after one pass.
Avoid ROSE because it is never useful.
Consider ROSE, use 21- or 22-gauge rather than 19-gauge, and perform four or more passes rather than three or fewer.
No coordination with pathology is needed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CHEST’s posted key recommendations suggest ROSE, a smaller 21/22-gauge needle over 19-gauge in suspected malignancy, and four or more passes over three or fewer. These are guideline-level recommendations, not a standalone procedure protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the Johns Hopkins Ko Pen Wang fellowship’s publicly posted clinical structure?

options.text: It is a six-month observership with no clinical training.
It posts 12 months of advanced clinical IP training, including advanced diagnostic bronchoscopy, therapeutic airway and pleural procedures, with an optional research year.
It publicly lists a fixed weekly rotation schedule and required case numbers.
It is a non-physician research certificate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official program page describes a 12-month clinical year in those domains and an optional 12-month research year. It does not publish a detailed rotation calendar or case log; those must not be invented.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which requirement is stated on the AABIP 2026 initial IP board-certification application page for the accredited-fellowship track?

options.text: Only a self-attested online course is required.
Completion of an accredited IP fellowship, an IP fellowship certificate and program-director attestation are required; procedure logs are not required for that application.
An ABIM IP certificate is already sufficient without fellowship training.
Any non-accredited fellowship is automatically accepted.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AABIP lists completion of an accredited IP fellowship, training certificate, and program-director attestation; it states procedure logs are not required. It also retains authority to amend criteria.

practiceQuestions.stem: As of the ABIM July 2026 pulmonary board summary, what was the status of a possible ABIM subspecialty certification in IP?

options.text: A live ABIM IP initial-certification examination was accepting applications.
It had been permanently rejected.
ABIM was continuing evaluation/potential development and outreach, including an Intent to Certify survey and possible practice pathways, for Board consideration.
AABIP certification had become an ABMS certificate automatically.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM’s July 2026 summary describes ongoing evaluation and potential development; it does not announce a live ABIM IP certificate or exam. AABIP’s certification must not be conflated with ABIM/ABMS certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which phrase matches the FDA PMA indication quoted for the Zephyr Endobronchial Valve System?

options.text: Any dyspnea due to COPD, regardless of imaging or physiology.
Bronchoscopic treatment of adults with hyperinflation associated with severe emphysema in regions of lung with little to no collateral ventilation.
Treatment of malignant central airway obstruction.
A replacement for lung-transplant evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The FDA approval letter states that indication. A labeled indication does not establish appropriateness for an individual, nor does it replace specialty selection, training, consent, or follow-up.

practiceQuestions.stem: The BTS pleural disease page identifies which set of topics as covered by the current 2023 guideline?

options.text: Spontaneous pneumothorax, undiagnosed unilateral pleural effusion, pleural infection, and pleural malignancy.
Only asthma and COPD.
Only mediastinal staging.
Only cardiac catheterization.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BTS page explicitly lists those four areas and describes the guidance as current/valid in 2023. Local policy and updated evidence may still govern practice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional course planner wants to count a public recording whose page shows a transcript but not its total runtime. What is the defensible ledger action?

options.text: Estimate runtime from the last transcript timestamp and count it as verified.
Use the uploader’s usual webinar length.
Record duration as unknown and exclude it from verified-hour totals until direct runtime evidence is observed.
Count it twice if it covers two units.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The course contract requires observed recording duration and de-duplication of video IDs. A transcript endpoint or plausible estimate is not verified duration evidence.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which content area is explicitly listed at 0.7% under procedural knowledge in the published AABIP IP Board blueprint?

options.text: Coding and billing for bronchoscopy.
Pleural procedures.
Navigational/robotic/cone-beam CT bronchoscopy.
Tracheobronchial stents.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The blueprint lists coding and billing for bronchoscopy at 0.7%; it also makes clear that the examination content can vary. The course treats coding as an awareness topic, not legal, payer, or billing advice.

title: Pulmonary and Critical Care Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced learner level: completed or near-completed medical-school core knowledge and internal-medicine-level cardiopulmonary, renal, infectious-disease, pharmacology, physiology, and ethics foundations.

Ability to interpret basic vital signs, arterial blood gas terminology, ECG/radiograph terminology, and clinical evidence; learners without this background should use the OpenStax foundation reading and supervised local teaching.

For any real clinical activity: only the learner’s accredited programme, supervisor, licence and institutional policy determine permissions. This course authorizes no patient care, procedure, image acquisition, medication selection, or clinical documentation.
No prerequisite in this self-study course satisfies ABIM or ACGME eligibility requirements.
objectives: Map pulmonary and critical-care learning to current ABIM Pulmonary Disease and Critical Care Medicine certification blueprints without claiming test prediction.
Use a mechanism-first approach to respiratory symptoms, respiratory failure, shock, and multi-organ critical illness.
Interpret PFT/ABG/ventilation/POCUS concepts with explicit quality, uncertainty and supervision limits.
Differentiate major obstructive, diffuse parenchymal, pleural, vascular, infectious, sleep, thoracic-oncology and transplant domains.
Check older lecture claims against dated current sources such as GOLD 2026, GINA 2026, CDC TB 2025, and applicable guidelines.
Distinguish knowledge of a procedure from supervised competence, credentialing, and patient-specific decision-making.
Use authentic de-identified images only under an explicit compatible licence and with source/DOI attribution.
Communicate goals-of-care, safety, equity and recovery considerations as educational reasoning, not personal medical advice.

units.title: Respiratory physiology, symptoms, and pulmonary-function reasoning
objectives: Apply a structured physiologic differential to dyspnea, cough, hypoxemia, and hypercapnia.
Interpret spirometry, lung volumes, diffusing capacity, arterial blood gases, and cardiopulmonary exercise data at a conceptual level; state when quality or context prevents interpretation.
Relate PFT/CPET interpretation to preoperative and outpatient reasoning without performing tests independently.
topics: Mechanics, gas exchange, V/Q mismatch, shunt, A–a gradient, oxygen transport
Spirometry, bronchodilator response, volumes, DLCO, flow-volume loops, ABGs, CPET
boardDomains: ABIM Pulmonary: Respiratory Physiology and Pulmonary Symptoms (4%)
ABIM Critical Care: pulmonary disease—respiratory failure and ventilation
units.casePractice: Use a fictional PFT/ABG vignette; then compare reasoning with the Hopkins physiology rotation description. No patient data, tracing, or independent clinical interpretation is supplied.
units.assessment: One written ABG/PFT interpretation with uncertainty statement; original question Q01.

units.title: Obstructive airway disease and bronchiectatic disorders
objectives: Differentiate asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, central airway obstruction, and common mimics using physiology and clinical pattern recognition.
Use current GINA and GOLD documents as update checkpoints rather than relying on older lecture recommendations.
Describe escalation logic and exacerbation evaluation without prescribing an individualized regimen.
topics: Asthma phenotypes, exacerbation, severe asthma and mimics
COPD diagnosis, stable disease, exacerbation prevention, rehabilitation and oxygen context
Bronchiectasis, CF, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, central airway lesions
boardDomains: ABIM Critical Care: airway disease (high relevance)
units.casePractice: Fictional fixed-versus-variable obstruction and recurrent-exacerbation cases; use only de-identified/open resources if imaging is desired.
units.assessment: Compare an asthma mimic and COPD exacerbation differential in a two-column table; original questions Q02–Q03.

units.title: Interstitial, occupational, and environmental lung disease
objectives: Organize ILD by exposure, autoimmune context, imaging pattern, pathology, and tempo.
Identify features that warrant multidisciplinary review rather than a single-test diagnosis.
Explain why an image pattern alone does not establish an individual diagnosis.
topics: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, CTD-ILD, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sarcoidosis
Cystic lung disease, drug/radiation-related disease, pneumoconiosis and inhalational injury
Multidisciplinary ILD reasoning and limitations of imaging
boardDomains: ABIM Pulmonary: Diffuse Parenchymal Lung Disease (10%)
ABIM Pulmonary: Occupational and Environmental Diseases (2%)
units.casePractice: Open-i search may be filtered to CT/X-ray and a displayed CC license; link to the source record rather than copying its image. TCIA cancer datasets are not substitutes for ILD cases.
units.assessment: Write a four-branch ILD differential from a fictional exposure/serology/HRCT summary; original question Q04.

units.title: Pleural disease, airways, and procedural decision boundaries
objectives: Classify pleural syndromes and construct a diagnostic/therapeutic decision pathway.
Recognize that ultrasound, thoracentesis, chest tubes, bronchoscopy, and airway procedures require supervised competency and local governance.
State indications, contraindications, complications, alternatives, and escalation questions without attempting a procedure.
topics: Effusions, empyema, pneumothorax, hemothorax, trapped lung/entrapment
Thoracentesis, chest tubes, bronchoscopy/EBUS, sedation, ultrasound guidance
Airway obstruction and massive hemoptysis framework
boardDomains: ABIM Pulmonary: Pleural Disease (5%), Neoplasia—interventional pulmonary topics
units.casePractice: Fictional pleural-fluid and risk-assessment case. Do not practice procedures on people or simulate credentialing.
units.assessment: Annotate a “stop/escalate” checklist for a fictional pleural procedure request; original question Q05.

units.title: Pulmonary vascular disease and thromboembolism
objectives: Distinguish thromboembolic, pulmonary arterial, left-heart, lung/hypoxia-associated, and multifactorial pulmonary hypertension frameworks.
Apply a risk-aware approach to suspected PE and right-ventricular failure in a fictional scenario.
Explain why specialist evaluation and hemodynamic context matter before labeling pulmonary hypertension subtype.
topics: Pulmonary hypertension groups, RV failure, hemodynamics
Acute chest syndrome and pulmonary vasculitis overview
boardDomains: ABIM Critical Care: pulmonary vascular disorders; cardiovascular/hemodynamic monitoring
units.casePractice: Fictional PE/RV-strain and pulmonary-hypertension classification exercises. No actual treatment recommendation is generated.
units.assessment: State the next discriminating data element in a fictional PH work-up; original question Q06.

units.title: Thoracic neoplasia, nodules, and transplantation
objectives: Frame lung nodule and suspected thoracic malignancy evaluation as staging, tissue, risk, and multidisciplinary decisions.
Describe high-level transplantation selection/complication domains without claiming transplant-center competence.
Use authentic, de-identified CT/PET datasets only within their specific license and provenance.
topics: Nodules, lung cancer staging, mediastinal evaluation, complications
Transplant selection, rejection, infection, malignancy, outcomes
units.casePractice: TCIA RIDER-LUNG-CT and LUNG-PET-CT-DX are authentic de-identified DICOM datasets with CC BY 4.0 shown on their collection records; use their DOI citation and never add identifiers or rehost outside the stated license.
units.assessment: Produce a fictional nodule-workup information map, separating diagnostic certainty from management decisions; original question Q07.

units.title: Pulmonary infection, immunocompromise, and antimicrobial stewardship
objectives: Differentiate CAP, HAP/VAP, aspiration, bronchiectasis-associated infection, TB/NTM, fungal disease, and infection in an immunocompromised host.
Use current CDC TB guidance as an update check; distinguish educational reasoning from patient-specific antimicrobial selection.
Integrate source control, testing quality, resistance, and stewardship concepts.
topics: TB, NTM, fungi, viral respiratory disease, immunocompromise
Antimicrobial PK/PD, resistance, infection prevention and stewardship
units.casePractice: Use a fictional immunocompromised host vignette and publicly documented guideline tables; do not create a patient-specific regimen.
units.assessment: Explain why susceptibility, drug interactions, and host context must precede a TB regimen decision; original question Q08.

units.title: Sleep-related breathing, neuromuscular disease, and chronic ventilatory failure
objectives: Recognize OSA, central sleep apnea, hypoventilation, and neuromuscular/chest-wall mechanisms.
Compare the roles and limits of polysomnography, home testing, MSLT, and MWT conceptually.
Identify when sleep/ventilation symptoms require supervised clinical assessment.
topics: OSA, central sleep apnea, altitude/Cheyne–Stokes patterns
Sleep tests, PAP concepts, outcomes and comorbidity
boardDomains: ABIM Pulmonary: Sleep Medicine, Neuromuscular and Skeletal (10%)
units.casePractice: Fictional sleep-study-summary comparison; no raw personal sleep data or independent PAP prescription.
units.assessment: Identify the appropriate test limitation in a fictional hypoventilation presentation; original question Q09.

units.title: Shock, sepsis, monitoring, and ICU triage
objectives: Distinguish cardiogenic, distributive, hypovolemic, and obstructive shock using physiology and a reassessment loop.
Apply the ABIM task emphasis: diagnosis/testing (40%), treatment/care decisions (50%), risk/prognosis (5%), and pathophysiology (5%).
Use the 2021 SSC as a dated evidence source and explicitly recognize evolving guidance and local protocols.
topics: Sepsis/septic shock, source control, fluids/vasopressors as concepts
ICU admission, team communication, quality and safety
boardDomains: ABIM Critical Care: Shock (15%), Cardiovascular Disorders (13%), Infectious Disease (10%)
units.casePractice: Fictional undifferentiated-shock timeline with serial reassessment; it is not a protocol for real resuscitation.
units.assessment: Explain the physiologic category before choosing a response in a fictional shock case; original question Q10.

units.title: Acute respiratory failure, ARDS, and ventilatory support
objectives: Differentiate hypoxemic and hypercapnic failure and connect mechanism to monitoring priorities.
Explain invasive/noninvasive ventilation, liberation, waveform, oxygenation, and complication concepts.
Use current guideline material to check older recordings; do not set ventilators for a patient.
topics: ARDS, pulmonary edema, asthma/COPD failure, airway emergency
Ventilator modes, VILI, auto-PEEP, liberation, NIV, tracheostomy
Oxygen devices, prone positioning/adjunct concepts, ECMO knowledge boundary
boardDomains: ABIM Critical Care: Pulmonary Disease (17%); mechanical ventilation (6% in expanded blueprint)
units.casePractice: Fictional ARDS physiology/waveform question; any real ventilator adjustment requires an appropriately credentialed clinical team.
units.assessment: Choose the safer reasoning step in a fictional ventilated-patient scenario; review Q10 explanation and a reflection on uncertainty.

units.title: Systemic critical illness and multi-organ integration
objectives: Integrate renal, endocrine/metabolic, cardiovascular, neurologic, hematologic/oncologic, GI/hepatic, toxicologic, and postoperative problems into ICU reasoning.
Interpret acid-base/electrolyte patterns with explicit assumptions and limitations.
Recognize that critical care coverage is broader than a pulmonary lecture series and prioritize high-relevance blueprint domains.
topics: ACS, arrhythmias, heart failure, monitoring; stroke, delirium, sedation
Liver failure/GI, coagulopathy/transfusion, oncology/immunosuppression, toxicology, surgery/trauma
boardDomains: ABIM Critical Care: renal/endocrine/metabolic (13%), cardiovascular (13%), neurologic (9%), GI (5%), heme/onc (5%), surgery (5%), pharmacology/toxicology (5%)
units.casePractice: Fictional multi-organ ICU handoff. No patient records are used; information gaps and consultation triggers must be named.
units.assessment: Construct a problem representation and rank three immediate knowledge gaps for a fictional case; Q01/Q10 plus faculty-reviewed discussion if used in a lawful local setting.

units.title: POCUS, ethics, safety, recovery, and systems practice
objectives: Describe the diagnostic—not autonomous procedural—role of critical-care ultrasound.
Apply safety, advance-care-planning, prognostication, and potentially nonbeneficial-treatment concepts with communication humility.
Plan recovery, rehabilitation, transitions, and quality-improvement questions after critical illness.
topics: Cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal and vascular POCUS limits
Delirium, sedation, goals of care, organ donation, confidentiality
ICU-acquired weakness, long-term outcomes, QI and health equity
boardDomains: ABIM Critical Care: Critical Care Ultrasound (2%), Research/Administration/Ethics (1%); cross-cutting health equity
units.casePractice: Fictional surrogate-meeting and POCUS-image-quality cases. POCUS scans must never be acquired or interpreted as a substitute for supervised practice.
units.assessment: Write a neutral goals-of-care communication opener and a POCUS limitation statement; no grading of real clinical performance.

units.title: Procedural knowledge, evidence appraisal, and capstone synthesis
objectives: Map procedures to ABIM “perform competently,” knowledge-standard, and opportunity-to-train boundaries where published.
Appraise evidence, bias, safety, and generalizability in a pulmonary/critical-care teaching claim.
Synthesize a case presentation with differential, uncertainty, source quality, and escalation/supervision boundaries.
topics: Bronchoscopy/BAL, transbronchial biopsy, EBUS, pleural and vascular procedures
ECMO, advanced airways, percutaneous tracheostomy: knowledge boundaries versus performance
Quality improvement, equity, research ethics, multidisciplinary conference format
boardDomains: ABIM pulmonary procedure policy; ABIM CCM research/administration/ethics; both blueprints’ diagnostic and care-decision tasks
units.casePractice: Capstone uses a fully fictional de-identified-style scenario or an approved CC-licensed TCIA dataset with its required DOI; no real patient record, clinical procedure, or unlicensed image reuse.
units.assessment: Submit a source-annotated fictional case map plus a “what this course cannot verify” statement.

assignment.title: Fictional PCCM synthesis portfolio
components: A 1-page physiology and differential map for a fictional acute respiratory-failure case, including data missingness and uncertainty.
A 1-page evidence update log that compares one older lecture claim with a current primary guideline/report; quote no protected text or exam content.
One TCIA or Open-i provenance statement: URL/DOI, licence, attribution, authenticity, and why the image must not be rehosted or treated as a real patient-care study.
A 5-minute fictional multidisciplinary handoff that explicitly states supervision/escalation and goals-of-care boundaries.
assignment.submissionBoundary: No real patient records, identifiers, clinical images outside their licence, proprietary questions, protected downloads, payment/enrolment, or real patient treatment plans.

formative: Unit retrieval prompts and original questions Q01–Q10
assessment.summative: Portfolio rubric: 30% problem representation/physiology, 25% source quality and date-checking, 20% differential and uncertainty, 15% ethics/safety/equity, 10% provenance and scope. This is an educational rubric only—not an ABIM score, procedural assessment, clinical competence assessment, or predictor of passing any examination.
assessment.passingClaim: No score in this independent course grants fellowship credit, board eligibility, certification, licence, procedure competence, or a guarantee of passing.

medical.boardStatus: ABIM publishes separate Pulmonary Disease and Critical Care Medicine certification examinations and policies. A combined fellowship may support a dual-certification pathway; it is not a third, single ABIM certificate named “Pulmonary and Critical Care.”
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Exact current ABIM boundary (date checked 2026-10-07): at application, ABIM requires prior ABIM Internal Medicine certification, requisite accredited fellowship training, documented clinical competence/procedural skills and professional behaviour, an unrestricted/unencumbered licence, and passing the relevant examination. For pulmonary/critical-care dual certification, ABIM states a minimum of 3 years of accredited combined training, including 18 months full-time clinical training and continuity clinic over the 3 years. Pulmonary exam may follow satisfactory completion of 2 years; critical-care exam follows completion of all 3. Pulmonary certification need not be achieved before the critical-care exam. This course confers none of these requirements and cannot determine an individual’s eligibility. ABIM policies govern at application and may change.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner reviews spirometry that shows a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio after acceptable manoeuvres. Which conclusion is most defensible before assigning a disease label?

options.text: The pattern supports airflow obstruction; clinical context, bronchodilator response, volumes, and DLCO may refine the differential.
The pattern proves asthma.
The pattern proves COPD.
Spirometry alone determines transplant eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A reduced ratio can support obstruction but does not uniquely diagnose asthma or COPD. ABIM expects interpretation of pulmonary testing within physiology and symptom reasoning; the course preserves the need for clinical context and test quality.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional severe-wheeze scenario, which study action best protects against importing an outdated recommendation from a recorded lecture?

options.text: Check the recording against the current GINA strategy report and record its update date.
Assume the oldest lecture is most authoritative.
Use a video comment as the guideline.
Copy a medication plan into a real patient chart.

practiceQuestions.rationale: GINA provides a current strategy report; recordings may predate updated evidence. This is an evidence-checking question, not a treatment instruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult with chronic symptoms has an obstructive pattern and recurrent infections. Which reasoning move is most appropriate?

options.text: Consider a differential that includes COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis-related disease when appropriate, and central airway processes rather than forcing one label.
Conclude that every obstructive pattern is COPD.
Ignore infection history because it is not pulmonary.
Perform bronchoscopy without supervision.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The pulmonary blueprint includes asthma, COPD, CF, non-CF bronchiectasis, and central airway obstruction/mimics. Procedures remain supervised training activities.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional HRCT summary has diffuse parenchymal abnormalities in a person with a potential exposure and autoimmune symptoms. What is the safest educational conclusion?

options.text: Build an exposure, autoimmune, tempo, imaging-pattern, and multidisciplinary differential; the summary alone does not establish a final diagnosis.
Name idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with certainty from one summary.
Discard the exposure history.
Generate a synthetic CT and call it confirmatory.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The blueprint spans CTD-ILD, idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, granulomatous disease, exposures, and rare disease. The course does not turn a description or generated image into diagnostic ground truth.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a new pleural effusion. Before thinking about a pleural procedure, which statement is correct for this course?

options.text: Learners should identify the diagnostic question, contraindications, alternatives, complication risk, and supervision requirement; the course does not confer procedural competence.
Watching a video grants thoracentesis privileges.
Ultrasound eliminates all complication risk.
All effusions have one cause.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM differentiates required performance, knowledge standards, and opportunity to train. Procedure competency is assessed in accredited training, not earned through this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional pulmonary-hypertension work-up, what prevents premature subtype labeling?

options.text: Integrate clinical setting, cardiac/lung disease context, thromboembolic evaluation, hemodynamics, and specialist assessment.
Use a single symptom to assign a group.
Assume all pulmonary hypertension is pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Rely on an unverified social-media clip.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM pulmonary and critical-care blueprints include pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary vascular disorders; they require diagnostic reasoning rather than a single-sign diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner wants to use a lung CT/PET case in a slide deck. Which source choice follows the course’s image-provenance rule?

options.text: Use a TCIA collection record that displays CC BY terms, retain required DOI attribution, and follow TCIA non-reidentification restrictions.
Copy any image found online because it is viewable.
Create a synthetic CT and label it a real patient scan.
Upload a real patient scan without authorization.

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA collection pages list licences and required data citations; the policy prohibits re-identification and sets access/attribution boundaries.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional person may have drug-susceptible pulmonary TB. Which information is explicitly relevant before selecting a regimen?

options.text: Susceptibility results, coexisting conditions, and possible drug–drug interactions.
Only the chest radiograph.
Only a generic online dose table.
Whether a lecture has a high view count.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC states that regimen selection depends on susceptibility, comorbidities, and interactions. This question does not provide or authorize an individual regimen.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional sleepy patient is suspected to have sleep-disordered breathing plus possible hypoventilation. Which is the most appropriate study habit?

options.text: Specify the suspected mechanism and the limitations/appropriate role of the proposed sleep or ventilatory test before interpreting it.
Treat every symptom as obstructive sleep apnea.
Read one tracing and prescribe therapy without clinical assessment.
Exclude neuromuscular and obesity-related hypoventilation from the differential.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The pulmonary blueprint includes OSA, central sleep apnea, testing, and hypoventilation from chest-wall, obesity, and neuromuscular disease.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional ICU case has hypotension, suspected infection, and worsening oxygenation. What is the best first reasoning frame in this course?

options.text: Classify possible shock physiology, identify time-critical reversible causes and source questions, reassess serial data, and use local supervised protocols for actual care.
Assume one measurement settles the diagnosis permanently.
Ignore oxygenation because the problem is circulatory.
Apply a generic video plan directly to the patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM gives major weight to shock, pulmonary disease, and infection; the SSC is a dated guideline source. The intended skill is structured, reassessable reasoning—not independent treatment.

Airway, respiratory physiology and ventilatory support concepts

Interventional pain, neuromodulation and complication awareness
Shock, sepsis, cardiac critical illness and mechanical support concepts
Acute respiratory failure, ultrasound and diagnostic uncertainty
Renal, metabolic and endocrine critical illness
Neurocritical illness, prognosis, infection and ethics
Evidence synthesis, recovery, equity and practice boundaries

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional outpatient adult has chronic low-back pain. Which CDC scope statement is accurate?

options.text: It is an inflexible legal maximum for every setting.
It is voluntary outpatient-adult guidance and excludes cancer-related pain, sickle-cell disease, palliative and end-of-life care.
It replaces ICU sedation guidance.
It is for pediatric postoperative care only.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC describes this outpatient scope and explicit exclusions; the fictional case does not call for a prescription decision.

It could not issue a recommendation for or against antipsychotics over usual care for delirium treatment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SCCM reports insufficient evidence for that comparison; other recommendations are conditional.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 pain requirements state the continuity-clinic and 50-patient elements; this course cannot fulfill them.

title: Anesthesiology Residency

prerequisites.recommendedLearnerLevel: Advanced medical/graduate-health-science independent study. This is not an admissions pathway, clinical credential, or substitute for medical school/residency.
knowledge: Foundational anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, pathophysiology, and clinical terminology.
Ability to read primary guidelines critically and distinguish dated educational recordings from current guidance.
safetyAndAccess: No learner may use this material to perform anesthesia, prescribe, supervise, or make a real-patient plan.
Use only openly accessible source links; do not download/rehost protected media or access proprietary examinations.
prerequisites.actualProgrammePrerequisiteBoundary: For a 36-month ACGME anesthesiology program, entrants must have completed 12 months of fundamental clinical-skills education in a qualifying program; ACGME describes 36- and 48-month formats. This course neither verifies nor supplies that prerequisite. See ACGME requirements and the Johns Hopkins applicant page.

objectives: Map independent-study topics to published ABA BASIC, ADVANCED, and APPLIED public content descriptions without claiming exam preparation suffices for eligibility.
Explain preanesthesia, monitoring, airway, pharmacology, regional/pain, recovery, organ-system, and subspecialty concepts using current primary sources.
Interpret fictional monitor, physiology, and communication scenarios while clearly distinguishing analysis from patient-specific decisions.
Locate and date-check ASA, ASRA, SOAP, ACGME, ABA, and institutional sources; identify when historical video material must be updated.
Communicate risk, consent, handoff, uncertainty, and QI issues in fictional formative exercises.

units.title: Professional scope, preanesthesia evaluation, consent, and risk framing
objectives: Distinguish educational preparation from supervised clinical authority and state what a preanesthesia evaluation includes.
Organize a focused risk narrative that separates known information, uncertainty, and escalation needs.
Practice an informed-consent conversation in plain language without making a patient-specific recommendation.
topics: medical-record review; prior anesthesia; focused interview/exam; relevant tests/consultation; anesthesia plan; consent; ethical limits
boardDomains: ABA BASIC—Clinical Sciences: Evaluation of the Patient & Preoperative Preparation
units.casePractice: Use a fictional preoperative vignette. Build a question list and handoff summary; do not create a patient-specific anesthetic plan.
units.assessment: 100–150 word structured preanesthesia note critique plus a two-minute role-play reflection, assessed only for source citation and explicit uncertainty.

units.title: Basic science: pharmacology, physics, delivery systems, and monitoring
objectives: Relate pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics and organ physiology to expected anesthetic effects.
Interpret the purpose and limits of monitoring and delivery-system checks.
Explain why objective neuromuscular monitoring and recovery criteria matter.
topics: IV/inhaled agents; opioids; local anesthetics; autonomic drugs; neuromuscular blockade; flow, vaporization, circuits; capnography; pulse oximetry; ECG; blood pressure
boardDomains: ABA BASIC—Basic Sciences (24%): pharmacology; physics, monitoring & delivery devices
units.casePractice: Use invented monitor traces and a manufacturer-neutral machine schematic; identify the information each signal can and cannot supply.
units.assessment: Ten-item formative interpretation set, including one train-of-four recovery explanation; no device operation or patient care.

units.title: Airway, respiration, general anesthesia, and ventilation reasoning
objectives: Identify airway-risk information and formulate a contingency-oriented airway strategy conceptually.
Explain respiratory physiology relevant to ventilation and oxygenation monitoring.
Recognize the difference between an airway algorithm discussion and performing an airway intervention.
topics: airway assessment; anticipated difficult airway; awake-versus-after-induction decision factors; oxygenation; ventilation; thoracic physiology; general anesthesia; sedation boundaries
boardDomains: ABA BASIC—Clinical Sciences: General Anesthesia, MAC/Sedation, Common Complications
units.casePractice: Fictional difficult-airway scenario: label risk factors, resources, backup pathways, and handoff communication. No procedural rehearsal on people.
units.assessment: Written branch-point map that cites the ASA difficult-airway source and names at least two uncertainties.

units.title: Fluid, blood, metabolic, renal, and endocrine considerations
objectives: Explain how fluid, hematologic, renal, and endocrine physiology can alter perioperative assessment.
Interpret broad categories of laboratory/monitoring data without prescribing treatment.
Recognize when a case requires supervised specialty or critical-care escalation.
topics: fluid compartments; electrolytes; acid-base concepts; coagulation concepts; renal and endocrine physiology; blood conservation principles
units.casePractice: Fictional trend table with volume, urine-output, and laboratory descriptors; distinguish observations from a treatment order.
units.assessment: Short-answer data interpretation with required statement: “This is study analysis, not a treatment recommendation.”

units.title: Cardiovascular, neurologic, pulmonary, and multisystem physiology
objectives: Integrate organ-system physiology with anesthetic monitoring priorities.
Compare mechanisms that can change oxygen delivery, ventilation, perfusion, and neurologic risk.
Communicate a concise systems-based differential for a simulated deterioration.
topics: cardiac function; circulation; pulmonary gas exchange; neurophysiology; renal/blood/endocrine physiology; multimorbidity
units.casePractice: Fictional perioperative monitor/data trend drill. List plausible physiologic categories before looking up a source; no diagnosis is asserted.
units.assessment: One-page mechanism map and source-checked correction log.

units.title: Regional anesthesia, acute pain, chronic pain, and medication safety
objectives: Describe indications, benefits, limitations, and consent considerations for regional/local analgesia at a conceptual level.
Identify why antithrombotic status and infection-risk guidance require current source checking.
Compare multimodal pain concepts without selecting an intervention for a real patient.
topics: regional techniques overview; local anesthetic pharmacology; acute pain service; chronic pain concepts; opioid stewardship; antithrombotic safety; fascial-plane guidance
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED—Clinical Sciences: Regional Anesthesia; Clinical Subspecialty: Painful Disease States
units.casePractice: Compare three fictional consent statements for clarity, uncertainty, and noncoercion; use no needle insertion or patient images.
units.assessment: Source-indexed risk/benefit comparison and a 300-word safety reflection.

units.title: Postanesthesia care, complications, and recovery systems
objectives: Explain the purpose of PACU/equivalent care, transfer communication, and recovery reassessment.
Identify monitoring domains emphasized during recovery.
Apply a structured escalation and disclosure framework to a fictional postoperative concern.
topics: transport; PACU admission; verbal handoff; oxygenation/ventilation/circulation/consciousness/temperature; discharge responsibility; postoperative complications
boardDomains: ABA BASIC—Postoperative Care and Common Complications
units.casePractice: Write a simulated PACU handoff with the minimum information needed to make an uncertainty visible.
units.assessment: Checklist-based peer review of the fictitious handoff; no clinical verification or competency sign-off.

units.title: Obstetric anesthesia and peripartum safety
objectives: Identify the distinct physiologic, analgesic, monitoring, and communication context of peripartum care.
Locate current SOAP/ASA sources rather than treating historical lectures as definitive.
Explain why obstetric issues require supervised obstetric-anesthesia systems.
topics: labor analgesia concepts; cesarean context; neuraxial respiratory-depression monitoring; thrombocytopenia/anticoagulation source awareness; enhanced recovery
units.casePractice: Fictional peripartum handoff and monitoring-priority exercise; specifically do not calculate dosing or authorize neuraxial care.
units.assessment: Two-source evidence update note, including a publication-date check.

units.title: Cardiac, neuro, thoracic, and geriatric subspecialty reasoning
objectives: Describe why subspecialty cases alter monitoring, physiology, and team communication needs.
Differentiate foundational familiarity from fellowship-level expertise.
Use an evidence ledger to flag older recordings for update before applying a concept.
topics: cardiac anesthesia concepts; TEE context; neuro/EEG concepts; thoracic physiology; aging/frailty; multidisciplinary coordination
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED—Cardiovascular, CNS, Respiratory systems; Geriatric Anesthesia/Aging
units.casePractice: Fictional cardiac/neuro/thoracic comparison table; tag which questions need a subspecialist or current local protocol.
units.assessment: A one-page “what I know / what needs supervision” reflection.

units.title: Pediatric anesthesia and developmental considerations
objectives: Recognize that pediatric airway, physiology, consent, and escalation differ from adult care.
Identify the educational boundary between learning concepts and performing pediatric procedures.
Find and evaluate a current pediatric-anesthesia resource before relying on historical review material.
topics: pediatric physiology; airway/respiratory risk concepts; developmental considerations; communication with caregivers; pediatric subspecialty pathway
units.casePractice: Fictional caregiver communication station; do not use a child, clinical image, or simulated invasive procedure.
units.assessment: Plain-language explanation evaluated against the ABA OSCE communication domains.

units.title: Critical care, trauma, non-OR, ambulatory, and systems transitions
objectives: Compare environmental constraints of non-OR, ambulatory, and critical-care settings.
Identify why equipment, transport, staffing, and escalation systems matter.
Separate a public rotation description from independently verified hands-on competence.
topics: remote anesthesia; ambulatory workflow; ICU concepts; trauma; transfer of care; environmental preparedness
boardDomains: ABA ADVANCED—Clinical Subspecialty: Critical Care, Trauma, Ambulatory Surgery
units.casePractice: Fictional remote-site readiness checklist; no actual setup or clinical operation.
units.assessment: Systems-hazard analysis with a cited escalation boundary.

units.title: Quality, ethics, well-being, emergency cognition, and APPLIED-style communication
objectives: Use patient-safety and quality-improvement language in a simulated event review.
Frame consent, ethical conflict, team communication, and professional well-being topics appropriately.
Practice oral organization and monitor interpretation only as a formative educational exercise.
topics: OSCE communication; SOE organization; ethics; QI; patient safety; emergency manuals; clinician well-being; handoffs
units.casePractice: Fictional disclosure/communication and QI station. It is not an ABA examination, clinical simulation credential, or professional assessment.
units.assessment: Five-minute recorded self-reflection using a rubric based on public ABA OSCE domains; delete recordings after personal review.

assignment.title: Source-checked fictional perioperative safety portfolio
deliverables: A 12-unit evidence log that identifies the current primary source used for each topic.
Three fictional exercises: preanesthesia information map; monitoring/airway uncertainty map; PACU handoff.
A 500-word update memo contrasting one historical lecture claim with a current primary source.
One non-recorded or self-deleted fictional consent/QI role-play reflection.
assignment.requirements: Use fictional scenarios only; no real patient records, patient images, local protocols, protected exam material, procedure performance, or patient-specific treatment plan. Every clinical assertion must have a date-checked source link.
assignment.gradingBoundary: Formative self-study only. No institutional grading, medical supervision, technical competency assessment, case credit, or credential is granted.

formativeComponents.name: Fictional case reasoning and uncertainty labels

assessment.passingOrCertification: None. Scores are personal study feedback only and are not a validated predictor of ABA performance, clinical competence, or patient outcomes.

studyHours.type: Transparent independent-study plan, not clinical training time
studyHours.note: No clinical rotation, call, simulation credential, procedure, supervised patient care, case log, or residency time is represented in these hours.

unitMap.text: Professional scope, preanesthesia evaluation, consent, and risk framing
coveredTopics: medical-record review; prior anesthesia; focused interview/exam; relevant tests/consultation; anesthesia plan; consent; ethical limits

unitMap.text: Basic science: pharmacology, physics, delivery systems, and monitoring
coveredTopics: IV/inhaled agents; opioids; local anesthetics; autonomic drugs; neuromuscular blockade; flow, vaporization, circuits; capnography; pulse oximetry; ECG; blood pressure

unitMap.text: Airway, respiration, general anesthesia, and ventilation reasoning
coveredTopics: airway assessment; anticipated difficult airway; awake-versus-after-induction decision factors; oxygenation; ventilation; thoracic physiology; general anesthesia; sedation boundaries

unitMap.text: Fluid, blood, metabolic, renal, and endocrine considerations
coveredTopics: fluid compartments; electrolytes; acid-base concepts; coagulation concepts; renal and endocrine physiology; blood conservation principles

unitMap.text: Cardiovascular, neurologic, pulmonary, and multisystem physiology
coveredTopics: cardiac function; circulation; pulmonary gas exchange; neurophysiology; renal/blood/endocrine physiology; multimorbidity

unitMap.text: Regional anesthesia, acute pain, chronic pain, and medication safety
coveredTopics: regional techniques overview; local anesthetic pharmacology; acute pain service; chronic pain concepts; opioid stewardship; antithrombotic safety; fascial-plane guidance

unitMap.text: Postanesthesia care, complications, and recovery systems
coveredTopics: transport; PACU admission; verbal handoff; oxygenation/ventilation/circulation/consciousness/temperature; discharge responsibility; postoperative complications

unitMap.text: Obstetric anesthesia and peripartum safety
coveredTopics: labor analgesia concepts; cesarean context; neuraxial respiratory-depression monitoring; thrombocytopenia/anticoagulation source awareness; enhanced recovery

unitMap.text: Cardiac, neuro, thoracic, and geriatric subspecialty reasoning
coveredTopics: cardiac anesthesia concepts; TEE context; neuro/EEG concepts; thoracic physiology; aging/frailty; multidisciplinary coordination

unitMap.text: Pediatric anesthesia and developmental considerations
coveredTopics: pediatric physiology; airway/respiratory risk concepts; developmental considerations; communication with caregivers; pediatric subspecialty pathway

unitMap.text: Critical care, trauma, non-OR, ambulatory, and systems transitions
coveredTopics: remote anesthesia; ambulatory workflow; ICU concepts; trauma; transfer of care; environmental preparedness

unitMap.text: Quality, ethics, well-being, emergency cognition, and APPLIED-style communication
coveredTopics: OSCE communication; SOE organization; ethics; QI; patient safety; emergency manuals; clinician well-being; handoffs

topicGaps: Ready recordings are principally historical review material (some 2014–2019) or segmented foundational lessons; they are not a current institutional lecture set.

No observed free full lecture was used as definitive current instruction for difficult-airway guidance, 2025 ASA monitoring standards, current neuromuscular guideline interpretation, or current regional/antithrombotic decisions. Primary sources are required alongside videos.
No video/case resource supplies supervised technical performance, operative judgment, case logs, local emergency systems, or current institutional protocol training.
The public Johns Hopkins pages do not publish complete resident lecture titles, individual recording durations, private simulation material, case volume, or a complete rotation calendar.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Study scope is the single, categorical Johns Hopkins Anesthesiology Residency named in the item packet. The directory’s “three years” is treated as the clinical-anesthesia portion, while the ACGME recognizes 36-month and 48-month formats and Hopkins describes a clinical base year. Excluded as separate variants: combined Emergency Medicine–Anesthesiology and combined Anesthesiology–Pediatrics. Critical Care Scholars and Research Scholars are published internal pathway/track variants, not proof of a separate categorical specialty, accreditation, board status, or a guarantee of fellowship placement.
sourceCaveats: The exact programme directory URL was read in full. It identifies an actual Anesthesiology Residency and ACGME status; it does not establish an individual learner’s status.

The public programme directory lists a three-year duration, while the public applicant page and ACGME requirements describe the clinical base year and 36-/48-month training configuration. This report preserves rather than erases that distinction.
ACGME training requirements, institutional rotation descriptions, ABA certification/exam materials, and this self-study course are different source types and are labeled as such.

originalClipPlan.title: Preanesthesia evaluation to recovery handoff: evidence-map walkthrough
objectives: Show how record review, focused assessment, monitoring concepts, and handoff are connected in a fictional case.
Make clear that the clip is not a protocol or a substitute for local policy.
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Original narration over a conceptual workflow diagram only; no patient record, dose, monitor screenshot, or procedural demonstration. Quote and link current ASA standards.

originalClipPlan.title: Difficult-airway strategy: branch points, oxygenation, and limits
objectives: Explain why a preformulated strategy distinguishes awake, ventilatable-but-difficult, cannot-ventilate/cannot-intubate, and rescue contingencies.

originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Original conceptual animation of decision branches with no patient imagery or step-by-step invasive technique. Cite the 2022 ASA guideline and monitoring standard.
originalClipPlan.gapAddressed: Airway strategy coverage is fragmented among ready lectures and historical material; topic gap only, not ready lecture time.

originalClipPlan.title: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring: interpreting the guideline, not prescribing care
objectives: Distinguish qualitative observations from quantitative monitoring concepts.
State the ASA emphasis on adductor-pollicis monitoring and TOF recovery threshold while avoiding patient-specific drug direction.
originalClipPlan.scriptOutline: Original schematic waveform/ratio teaching graphic with fictional values and no clinical device operation. Link to ASA source.
originalClipPlan.gapAddressed: The observed recordings predate current guidance in places; current NMB interpretation is a topic gap only.

originalClipPlan.title: OSCE communication and safety disclosure: a fictional station debrief
objectives: Model lay-language explanation, questions, uncertainty, and noncoercive confirmation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult is receiving general anesthesia. Which monitoring interval is explicitly stated in the ASA basic monitoring standard for evaluation of arterial blood pressure and heart rate?

options.text: At least every 1 minute
At least every 5 minutes
At least every 15 minutes
Only at incision and emergence

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current ASA standard states that arterial blood pressure and heart rate are determined and evaluated at least every five minutes during anesthesia. This item tests the published standard, not an instruction for a real case.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional general-anesthesia scenario in which an endotracheal tube has been inserted, what does the ASA monitoring standard require for position verification?

options.text: Chest radiograph alone
Clinical assessment plus identification of carbon dioxide in expired gas
Pulse oximetry alone
Auscultation alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASA states correct ETT or supraglottic-airway positioning must be verified by clinical assessment and identification of expired carbon dioxide; it also specifies continual quantitative end-tidal CO2 analysis from placement until removal/transfer, subject to its stated circumstances.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional cooperative patient is suspected to be difficult to intubate and difficult to ventilate by face mask or supraglottic airway. Which concept is most consistent with the 2022 ASA difficult-airway guideline?

options.text: Proceed with repeated attempts after induction without a strategy
When appropriate, consider awake intubation and have a preformulated strategy
Avoid supplemental oxygen during airway management
Use one device only regardless of failure

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline recommends a preformulated strategy and, when appropriate, awake intubation when difficult intubation plus difficult ventilation is anticipated, among other conditions. Actual decisions require clinician judgment, patient factors, and resources.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which current ASA source-based statement best describes objective neuromuscular recovery in a fictional extubation discussion?

options.text: A train-of-four ratio of 0.5 confirms recovery
Quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis with train-of-four ratio at least 0.9 before extubation is emphasized
Quantitative monitoring has no role if the patient appears awake
All patients require the same pharmacologic antagonist

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASA’s guideline page emphasizes quantitative adductor-pollicis monitoring and TOF ratio ≥0.9 before extubation; it also frames antagonism in relation to block depth and agent. This is a conceptual source-check item, not medication direction.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which action belongs in the ASA basic preanesthesia-care standard before delivery of anesthesia care?

options.text: Review the available medical record and perform an appropriate interview/focused examination
Guarantee a complication-free outcome
Eliminate the need for consent
Order every possible laboratory test

practiceQuestions.rationale: The standard lists record review, interview/focused examination, pertinent tests/consultations as necessary, medications as appropriate, and ensuring consent. It does not prescribe indiscriminate testing or guarantee outcomes.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient is transported after anesthesia. Which statement best matches the ASA postanesthesia-care standard?

options.text: Postanesthesia management is optional after regional anesthesia
A PACU or equivalent must be available, and transfer includes reevaluation and verbal report
Only the surgeon may receive handoff information
Monitoring ceases upon leaving the OR

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASA requires appropriate postanesthesia management for general, regional, or MAC; a PACU/equivalent should be available, and the arriving patient is reevaluated with a verbal report to the responsible nurse.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which ABA BASIC blueprint category carries the largest relative percentage in the published blueprint?

options.text: Basic Sciences (24%)
Clinical Sciences (36%)
Organ-Based Basic & Clinical Sciences (37%)
Special Problems or Issues (3%)

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published ABA BASIC blueprint lists Organ-Based Basic & Clinical Sciences at 37%, narrowly above Clinical Sciences at 36%. Blueprint weights guide study organization; they are not a claim that this course predicts an examination result.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional consent station, which behavior is explicitly aligned with the ABA OSCE outline?

options.text: Use jargon and discourage questions
Explain indications, options, benefits/risks in lay terms, elicit questions, and confirm a voluntary decision
Promise a specific outcome
Obtain consent without discussing alternatives

practiceQuestions.rationale: The public ABA OSCE outline describes explaining options and relevant risks in lay terms, eliciting questions, responding appropriately, and confirming an affirmative decision without coercion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner wants one universal interval for all neuraxial procedures in patients receiving antithrombotic therapy. What is the most defensible learning response?

options.text: Use a memorized interval without reviewing the agent or current guidance
Recognize that rare hemorrhagic complications and agent-specific factors require current evidence-based guidance and supervised clinical judgment
Assume antithrombotics never matter for regional techniques
Use a video title as the only source

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASRA’s fifth-edition update explains that recommendations synthesize evidence, pharmacology, risk factors, and expert experience because spinal hematoma is rare. This question intentionally avoids inventing an interval or giving patient-specific advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes the scope of this independent curriculum relative to the ABA APPLIED examination?

options.text: Completion grants APPLIED eligibility
Its fictional oral/OSCE-style exercises are formative only; ABA APPLIED follows residency and ADVANCED-exam requirements
It replaces ABA registration
It certifies technical skills

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABA states APPLIED includes SOE and OSCE and is taken after passing ADVANCED; the public ADVANCED page says the physician takes it after completing residency and passing BASIC. This course has no affiliation, testing role, or eligibility authority.
